transcript.text: Sometimes when I open the dishwasher there's grey smelly water in the bottom even though it finished draining fine. Not every day though. Kitchen sink was replaced last month if that matters.

The sink replacement very likely matters. This is a classic symptom of a dishwasher drain hose that lost its "high loop" during the install.

## What's probably happening

The dishwasher drains into the sink plumbing (usually the garbage disposal or a branch tailpiece). To keep dirty sink water from flowing backward into the dishwasher, the drain hose needs to rise up high under the countertop before it drops down to the connection. Plumbers often take the hose down or reroute it when swapping a sink and don't put the loop back.

Without it, when you run water in the sink, drain a full basin, or run the disposal, that grey water can flow back through the hose and settle in the bottom of the dishwasher. That explains why:
• The dishwasher itself drains fine
• It only happens some days (depends on how much you used the sink)
• The water is grey and smelly (it's sink/disposal water, not dishwasher water)

## How to check

1. Look under the sink and follow the dishwasher drain hose (ribbed, usually grey or white) from the floor of the cabinet to where it connects.
2. Does it go up high first? It should be secured as close to the underside of the countertop as possible, ideally above the drain connection point, before dropping down. If it just runs low and straight across, that's your problem.
3. Also check if you have an air gap, a small chrome cylinder on the sink deck or countertop. If you had one before and it's gone, or the hoses aren't connected to it properly, that can cause the same issue.
4. Check where the hose connects. It must connect above the P-trap (to the disposal inlet or a dishwasher tailpiece), never below or after the trap.

## The fix

• High loop: Lift the hose as high as it will go and fasten it to the underside of the counter or the cabinet's back wall with a zip tie, hose clamp, or screw-in strap. This takes about 5 minutes and costs nothing.
• Air gap: If your local code requires one (some areas do), make sure it's installed and the hoses run correctly: dishwasher → air gap → disposal/tailpiece.
• If the connection is below the trap, that needs to be re-plumbed, and it's worth calling back whoever installed the sink.

## Other things to rule out

• Clogged filter at the bottom of the dishwasher: twist it out and rinse it. This can leave standing water, though usually it's present after every cycle.
• Partially clogged sink drain: If the sink drains slowly, backflow gets worse. Clearing it helps.

To confirm the diagnosis, run a full sink of water and drain it all at once, or run the disposal for a while, then open the dishwasher. If grey water appears, it's backflow, and the high loop or air gap fix should solve it.

I had a look under the sink. Since the new sink went in, the dishwasher hose just lies along the cupboard floor and goes straight into the waste spigot, with no high loop at all. I'll try looping it up high and clipping it, then let you know.

That's almost certainly the culprit. A hose lying flat into the waste spigot means sink water can run straight back into the dishwasher.

## Tips for doing the loop

• Go as high as you can. Aim for the underside of the worktop, or at least well above the spigot. Higher is better.
• Secure it firmly. A screw-in pipe clip or a cable tie looped through a small screw eye works well. If you use a cable tie, don't pull it so tight that it crushes the hose.
• Avoid kinks. Make a smooth, gentle curve rather than a sharp bend, which can slow draining or cause the dishwasher to throw an error.
• Check the connection while you're there. Make sure the hose is pushed fully onto the spigot and held with a jubilee clip or the clip it came with. Also check the spigot is above the trap. It usually is on a tailpiece, but worth a glance.

## Clearing out the old smell

Once it's looped:
1. Sponge out any standing water from the bottom of the dishwasher.
2. Pull out and rinse the filter. Sink gunk tends to collect there.
3. Run an empty hot cycle, either with a dishwasher cleaner or a cup of white vinegar upright on the top rack.

## How to tell it's worked

Over the next week, try the things that used to trigger it: draining a full sink, or running the tap hard. If the dishwasher stays dry, you're sorted.

If grey water still appears after a proper high loop, the next things to look at would be a partial blockage in the sink waste or trap (making water back up under pressure) or a faulty non-return valve in the dishwasher. But I'd expect the loop to fix it.

Let me know how it goes.
Done it - looped the hose up high and clipped it, and there's been no more water since. Cleaned the filter too, it was clean already.

Great, that confirms it was backflow from the sink.

A couple of small things worth keeping in mind:

• Mention it to whoever fitted the sink, so they know for future jobs, especially if they're doing other work for you.
• Give the clip a glance now and then, particularly after you've been rummaging in that cupboard. Hoses can get knocked down by bins or cleaning supplies.
• If you ever have the sink or dishwasher worked on again, check the loop is still there afterwards. It's the bit that most often gets missed.

If any lingering smell hangs around, one more hot empty cycle with vinegar should clear it.
